glossary.Dermis: The layer of skin under the epidermis, containing blood vessels, nerves and mast cells.
glossary.Superficial dermis: The upper part of the dermis, where the leak that makes urticarial wheals happens.
glossary.Deeper dermis: The lower dermis; swelling here, with subcutaneous tissue, gives angioedema.
glossary.Subcutaneous tissue: The fatty layer beneath the skin.
glossary.Vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels, causing redness and warmth.
glossary.Capillary permeability: How leaky the smallest vessels are; histamine raises it so fluid escapes.
glossary.Transient: Short-lived; each urticarial wheal fades within 24 hours.
glossary.Dermal swelling: Fluid collecting within the skin layer, raising a wheal.
glossary.Autoimmune: Caused by the immune system attacking the body's own tissues.
glossary.Autoantibodies: Antibodies made against the body's own molecules, here IgE or its receptor.
glossary.Aspirin: An NSAID antiplatelet drug that can trigger or worsen urticaria.
glossary.Non-sedating antihistamine: A second-generation antihistamine that barely enters the brain, so causes little drowsiness.
glossary.Sedating antihistamine: An older antihistamine that crosses into the brain and causes drowsiness.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: a blood marker of inflammation.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: a slow-changing blood marker of inflammation.
glossary.Trigger-directed workup: Tests chosen to look for the specific cause the history suggests.
glossary.Monoclonal antibody: A lab-made antibody aimed at one specific target molecule.
glossary.Anti-IgE: Binds and removes free IgE so it cannot arm mast cells.
glossary.CNS: Central nervous system: the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.Competitively block: Occupy a receptor so the natural chemical, here histamine, cannot bind.
glossary.Downregulate: Reduce the number of receptors on a cell's surface.
glossary.Wheeze: High-pitched whistling on breathing out from narrowed airways.
glossary.Hypotension: Low blood pressure; with urticaria it suggests anaphylaxis.
glossary.Autoimmune thyroid disease: Thyroid disorders such as Hashimoto's caused by autoantibodies; more common in chronic urticaria.
glossary.Functional distress: Upset and disruption to daily life, work and sleep caused by symptoms.
glossary.Specialist therapies: Treatments started by a dermatology or allergy specialist when standard drugs fail.
glossary.Contact allergies: Reactions to substances touching the skin, such as latex or cosmetics.
glossary.Free IgE: IgE circulating unbound in the blood, available to attach to mast cells.
